segments.voice: Yesterday, hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna, and Ushas, the dawn: those who saw her before are gone, we see her now, and others will. Did you give the sky one breath this morning? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.
screen: `THEY SAW HER; WE SEE HER; OTHERS WILL.`

segments.voice: A friend stops answering. No fight. No reason given. The messages just go unread. So the scrolling starts: back through the thread, looking for the line that went wrong. Then the asking around. Did they say anything to you? A hymn in the Rig Veda, book seven, follows almost exactly those steps. Only the one who has gone quiet is Varuna, the god who keeps the order of the world. Today: the fourth voice, and the hymn of someone asking what they did.
screen: `A FRIEND GOES QUIET.` → `SCROLLING BACK FOR THE WRONG LINE.` → `THE ONE GONE QUIET IS VARUNA.`

segments.voice: Varuna, in the Rig Veda, is the keeper of rita, the order that holds the world together: the sun on its path, the rivers in their beds, truth between people. He sees what's done in secret. Tradition gives book seven to the family of the sage Vasishtha, and hymn eighty-six there is a singer's plea to Varuna. It opens in wonder at Varuna's greatness. Then it turns personal. In paraphrase: when will I be close to Varuna again? Will he accept my offering without anger? Then the singer goes looking for the cause. I ask, wanting to know my wrong, he says. I go to the wise and ask them. And the wise all give the same answer: Varuna is angry with you. So he asks Varuna directly. What was my great offense, that you would strike down your friend, the one who praises you? Tell me, so I can come to you, free of it. Then come two remarkable verses. He asks to be released from what his fathers did and from what he has done himself, as a calf is untied from its rope. And he names the causes plainly, in paraphrase: it wasn't my own will. It was drink, anger, dice, thoughtlessness. Some readers hear an excuse in that line. Others hear an honest naming of what pulls a person off course. Either way, the hymn doesn't wallow. It asks, it listens, it names what went wrong, and it asks to be untied. And the singer calls himself Varuna's friend, the one who praises him. That's the shape of the plea: not a stranger begging, but a friend asking to be close again.
screen: `VARUNA, WHO KEEPS THE ORDER.` · `"WHAT WAS MY WRONG?"` · `UNTIED, LIKE A CALF FROM A ROPE.` · `DRINK, ANGER, DICE, THOUGHTLESSNESS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: untie one knot. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one thing you did that put some distance between you and someone else, or between you and what you hold right. Not the worst thing. A small one. Look at what was behind it, the way the singer did: tiredness, anger, a distraction, a moment of not thinking. Name it to yourself, plainly. Then picture a rope loosening, a little at a time, with each out-breath. If you pray, you can ask, in your own way, to be close again. The bell holds the time.

Hymns to Agni, and today, to Varuna, keeper of the world's order. In Rig Veda seven, eighty-six, a singer asks what he did wrong, names it, and asks to be untied like a calf from its rope. Today's word.
Your line: hymns to Agni, Indra, Ushas, Varuna. Today, if someone has gone quiet on you, ask them plainly what went wrong, and listen. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Hymns to Varuna are kept in Vedic recitation; in later Hindu tradition Varuna is honored as lord of the waters.

original.note: Sanskrit: the order of the world, of truth and of right action, which Varuna keeps in the Rig Veda.

trapdoor: what you thought: Varuna is a far-off sky god.
what it means: in Rig Veda 7.86, Varuna is close enough to miss, and the singer asks to be his friend again.
what a scholar hears: verse six, na sa svo daksho varuna dhrutih sa: it was not my own will, Varuna; it was drink, anger, dice, thoughtlessness.

sources.ref: Rig Veda 7.86 (the singer's plea: when will I be close to Varuna? asking the wise; what was my offense? release us like a calf from its rope; not my own will: drink, anger, dice, thoughtlessness)
Rig Veda (Varuna as keeper of rita)

notes: RV 7.86 paraphrased from memory (vv. 2–6). Confirm: the wise all saying Varuna is angry (v. 3); 'what was my chief offense that you would slay your friend' (v. 4); release from the fathers' wrongs and our own, like a calf from its rope (v. 5; the text also has 'like a cattle thief'); 'not my own will: liquor, anger, dice, thoughtlessness' (v. 6). The trapdoor's Sanskrit 'na sa svo daksho varuna dhrutih sa' should be checked.
Book seven attributed to the Vasishtha family 'by tradition'; confirm.
Varuna as keeper of rita and seeing what is done in secret: general Rig Vedic picture (e.g. RV 1.25, 7.86–89); confirm.
Days 1268–1271 took Agni, Indra, Ushas and Varuna in turn; day 1272 (another writer) continues the title with paired gods.

Editor pass: 'the hymn doesn't make excuses' contradicted the quoted 'it wasn't my own will', so the line now gives both readings (excuse, or honest naming); 'calls himself Varuna's friend the whole way through' overclaimed (the word comes in v. 4) and was cut back in the teach, match and myth.
